title: Drivetrain Layouts
summary: Front-, rear- and all-wheel drive differ in which wheels push the car and where the heavy parts sit. Compare packaging, traction, handling balance and efficiency, and see how weight transfer decides which layout grips best when accelerating.

seo.title: FWD vs RWD vs AWD: Drivetrain Layouts Explained
seo.description: Front-, rear- and all-wheel drive compared: which wheels push the car, where the engine and gearbox sit, and how layout affects traction and handling.

learningObjectives: Describe front-, rear- and all-wheel-drive layouts and their main components
Explain how longitudinal weight transfer affects traction under acceleration
Compare the packaging and handling traits of each layout
Distinguish part-time four-wheel drive from permanent all-wheel drive
beginnerExplanation:
Every car has to get power from the engine to the road, but designers choose which wheels do the pushing. Most everyday cars use front-wheel drive: the engine sits sideways at the front with the gearbox and differential bolted to it, driving the front wheels through two short shafts. It is compact and leaves lots of cabin space.

Rear-wheel drive puts the engine lengthways and sends power down a long propeller shaft to a differential at the back. It spreads weight more evenly and frees the front wheels to concentrate on steering, which is why many sports and luxury cars and most heavy vans use it. All-wheel drive adds hardware so both axles can be driven, which helps on slippery roads and when accelerating hard.

When a car accelerates, weight shifts backwards, pressing the rear tyres down and lightening the front. That helps rear-wheel-drive cars launch and makes front-wheel-drive cars more likely to spin their tyres when pulling away briskly. Each layout is a set of compromises rather than a single 'best' choice.
technicalExplanation:
Front-engine front-drive (FF) cars usually mount the engine transversely with an integrated transaxle and unequal or equal-length half-shafts (an intermediate shaft equalises lengths to limit torque steer). Front weight bias of around 60% gives stable, understeer-biased handling and good traction in snow when cruising, but the front tyres must both steer and drive, so their friction budget is shared. Front-engine rear-drive (FR) cars use a longitudinal engine, gearbox, propshaft and rear axle; weight distribution can approach 50:50, and some place the gearbox at the rear axle (transaxle) for balance. Mid- and rear-engined layouts concentrate mass near the driven axle for traction and low yaw inertia.

Under acceleration a the load on the rear axle rises by ΔF = m a h / L, where h is the centre-of-gravity height and L the wheelbase. For a 1,500 kg car with h = 0.55 m and L = 2.7 m accelerating at 3 m/s², roughly 920 N moves from front to rear. Because tyre grip rises with load, the driven axle that gains load can transmit more force, so RWD and AWD out-launch FWD for a given power.

All-wheel drive needs a way for front and rear axles to turn at slightly different average speeds. Permanent systems use a centre differential (open, limited-slip or torque-sensing) with a fixed nominal split; on-demand systems drive one axle and engage the other through an electronically controlled multi-plate coupling. Traditional part-time 4WD locks front and rear axles together through a transfer case with an optional low range; it should only be used on loose surfaces, because on high-grip tarmac the locked axles fight each other in corners ('wind-up'). Electric vehicles add another option: separate motors on each axle, with no mechanical link between them at all.

steps.title: Front-wheel drive
steps.beginner: Engine, gearbox and differential sit together at the front and drive the front wheels — compact and space-efficient.
steps.technical: Transverse powertrain with an integrated transaxle; front tyres share their friction budget between steering and driving, giving understeer at the limit.

steps.title: Rear-wheel drive
steps.beginner: A long propeller shaft carries drive to a differential at the back; the front wheels only steer.
steps.technical: Longitudinal engine, gearbox, propshaft and rear axle allow near 50:50 balance and better launch traction; power can be used to adjust the car's attitude.

steps.title: Weight moves when you accelerate
steps.beginner: Accelerating presses the rear tyres harder into the road and lightens the front.
steps.technical: ΔF_rear = m a h / L. With m = 1,500 kg, a = 3 m/s², h = 0.55 m, L = 2.7 m, about 920 N transfers rearwards.

steps.title: All-wheel drive
steps.beginner: Both axles can be driven, so the car can use the grip of all four tyres.
steps.technical: Permanent AWD uses a centre differential; on-demand AWD engages the secondary axle through a controlled clutch coupling based on slip and driver inputs.

steps.title: Part-time 4WD
steps.beginner: Off-road vehicles can lock front and rear together and add an extra-low gear for steep, slippery ground.
steps.technical: A transfer case with no centre differential locks axle speeds; on grippy surfaces this causes driveline wind-up, so it is for loose terrain only.

keyConcepts.definition: Load moves from the front axle to the rear when accelerating (and the reverse when braking).
A gearbox and differential combined in one housing, standard in front-drive cars.
Lets the front and rear axles turn at different average speeds in permanent all-wheel drive.
Stress built up when axles are locked together but need to turn at different speeds, as in part-time 4WD on tarmac.

misconceptions.myth: All-wheel drive helps you stop and steer on ice.
misconceptions.reality: AWD only helps put power down. Braking and cornering grip depend on the tyres, which is why winter tyres matter more than driven wheels.

misconceptions.myth: Rear-wheel-drive cars are useless in snow.
misconceptions.reality: Modern traction and stability control, sensible weight distribution and good winter tyres make RWD cars perfectly usable; tyres dominate winter grip.

misconceptions.myth: Part-time 4WD can be left engaged all the time.
misconceptions.reality: Without a centre differential, locked axles fight each other on grippy roads, stressing the driveline and scrubbing the tyres.

practicalExamples: A powerful front-drive car may tug at the steering wheel under hard acceleration — torque steer from unequal driveshaft angles and loads.
Pulling away uphill on a wet road, a front-drive car spins its wheels sooner because load has moved off the front axle.
Many crossover SUVs are front-drive most of the time and engage the rear axle through a clutch only when front wheels begin to slip.

quiz.prompt: Why does a rear-drive car usually have better traction when accelerating hard from rest?
options: Weight transfers onto the rear driven wheels
The front wheels are lighter by design
quiz.explanation: Acceleration moves load rearwards (ΔF = m a h / L), increasing the grip available at the rear tyres.

quiz.prompt: A 1,500 kg car with h = 0.5 m and L = 2.5 m accelerates at 2 m/s². How much load moves to the rear axle?
When should a part-time 4WD system without a centre differential be engaged?
quiz.explanation: On loose surfaces the tyres can slip slightly to relieve wind-up; on grippy roads the locked axles fight each other.

faq.question: What is the difference between FWD, RWD and AWD?
faq.answer: Front-wheel drive sends power to the front wheels, which also steer; rear-wheel drive sends it to the rear wheels; all-wheel drive can drive all four. The choice changes packaging, weight distribution, traction and how the car behaves near its limits.

faq.question: Why are most small cars front-wheel drive?
faq.answer: Mounting the engine across the car, with the gearbox and differential combined in one transaxle, puts the whole drivetrain at the front. There is no propshaft running back, which saves weight, cost and cabin space, and the engine's weight over the driven wheels helps traction.

faq.question: Is all-wheel drive better in snow?
faq.answer: All-wheel drive helps you pull away and accelerate on slippery roads because the drive is shared between four tyres. It does not help you stop or corner, which depends on the tyres' grip, so good winter tyres matter more.
